conclusion: Enumerating the possible trait-sharing configurations becomes computationally prohibitive as the number of traits grows.
scope: Motivation for sequential discovery of configurations.
span: The challenge in multi-trait colocalization is that the configuration space grows combinatorially with the number of traits. At each locus with M putative causal variants that may influence two or more of L traits, enumerating all possible colocalization events requires evaluating M × (2L − 1) configurations. This combinatorial explosion becomes computationally prohibitive as the number of traits increases.

span: ColocBoost extends single-trait PSGB to multiple traits through Single-Effect Couplers (SEC). At each boosting iteration, a SEC evaluates whether traits share a common causal effect and, if so, performs coupled proximity-smoothed updates (Figure S1). The coupling decision is made locally by comparing joint versus separate trait updates using profile log-likelihood. Over successive iterations, these decisions progressively refine which traits are coupled, and the resulting trait groupings define the causal configuration T(s).

conclusion: Unlike mvSuSiE with a genome-wide learned sharing prior, ColocBoost learns local trait-sharing configurations through proximity-smoothed updates, SEC decisions, and adaptive scheduling.
scope: Author-stated distinction in statistical targets and computational constructions.
span: Multi-trait fine-mapping like mvSuSiE84 identifies variants that contribute globally to at least one trait, whereas ColocBoost, a multi-trait colocalization method, elucidates local colocalization events and the specific configuration of traits sharing each effect. Compared to mvSuSiE which fits a multivariate regression with a genome-wide estimated prior on effect-sharing patterns, ColocBoost, as a multi-task learning model, learns local sharing patterns through weak proximity-smoothed updates, SEC decisions across traits, and adaptive scheduling, providing a more flexible framework to identify heterogeneous effects across traits not captured by global Bayesian priors.
